title: Can a digital self-help tool, created together with autistic people, support them in managing headaches?
official: Feasibility of a co-designed digital self-management intervention for autistic individuals with headache: a mixed methods study.
summary:
Background and study aims
Headaches are very common and can make everyday life difficult. Research suggests autistic people get headaches more often than other people, but they are rarely included in headache research. Apps that help people manage their own headaches already exist, but they are designed for the general population and may not suit autistic people without changes.
This study works with autistic people to adapt an existing headache self-management app so that it suits autistic users better. The aim is to find out whether the app and the study itself are practical and acceptable. This is an early study to help plan a larger one in the future.

Who can participate?
Autistic people aged 16 and over who have frequent or long-lasting headaches (headaches at least once a month, for three months or more). A formal autism diagnosis is not needed, and people who identify as autistic are welcome. For the app part of the study, people need a smartphone or tablet they can use regularly.

What does the study involve?
There are two parts, and people can take part in one or both.
In Phase 1, participants take part in one interview lasting 45 to 90 minutes, online or in person at Ulster University. They share their experiences of headaches and what they would want from an app. A group that includes autistic members then helps design the app.
In Phase 2, participants use the app for 12 weeks on their own phone or tablet. For the first two weeks they only track their headaches. After that they can use short lessons on topics like sleep, pacing, relaxation and managing headache attacks. Participants fill in a short survey at the start and end, and may be invited to a short interview at the end. We offer vouchers as a thank-you.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating?
There is no promised personal benefit, but what participants share will shape the app. Talking about pain or health, or tracking headaches closely, can sometimes feel upsetting, and some people notice their headaches more while tracking them. Breaks, support information and a paper alternative to the app are available. The app does not give medical advice and does not replace care from a GP.

Where is the study run from?
Ulster University (UK).

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for?
The study is expected to start recruiting in autumn 2026, once ethical approval is in place, and to run until March 2028.

Who is funding the study?
A Physiotherapy Research Foundation (PRF) award, managed by the Chartered Society of Physiotherapy Charitable Trust (UK).

Who is the main contact?
Dr Joanne Marley, j.marley@ulster.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Age 16 or older
2. Formal autism diagnosis or self-identification as autistic
3. Persistent primary headache disorder or cervicogenic headaches
4. Persistent defined as:
4.1. Episodic  (1 to 14 days per month) 
4.2. Chronic (15 or more days per month) headache for 3 months or more
Exclusion criteria:
1. Currently enrolled in another headache or pain intervention trial
2. New headache, or symptoms suggestive of serious pathology (red flags, or secondary headaches other than cervicogenic)
3. Acute mental health (for example, very recent hospital admission or active care from a crisis team)
4. Photosensitive epilepsy, or epilepsy where the participant has been advised against the use of mobile screen-based apps
